chapters.title: Chapter 5: Proofs, Pitfalls and Real Choices

lessons.title: Investment Declarations, Proof Submission and What Happens If You Miss Them

children.text: Sneha, a business analyst in Pune, did everything right in April. She chose the old regime, declared her ₹25,000 monthly rent, ₹78,000 of ELSS SIPs and a ₹25,000 health insurance premium. Her TDS was a comfortable ₹8,580 a month. Then she missed the payroll email about the 15 January proof deadline. Her February payslip showed TDS of ₹41,913.

She had not lost her deductions. She had just failed to prove them to her employer on time. This lesson explains the annual declaration and proof cycle, the new forms under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, and exactly what happens, and how to recover, when you miss a step.

body.text: A declaration sets your TDS. A proof protects it. Your tax return settles it.

body.title: Tax year 2026-27: what you submit, and when

events.title: Tell your employer your tax regime
events.description: The new regime is the default. If you want TDS under the old regime, you must tell your employer in writing, usually through the payroll portal.

events.title: Declare expected claims in Form 124
events.description: Old regime: rent and landlord details, LTA, home loan interest and deductions like Section 123 (old 80C) and Section 126 (old 80D). TDS is calculated on these estimates.

events.title: Report previous employer salary in Form 122
events.description: If you changed jobs during the year, declare salary and TDS from your earlier employer, plus any other income you want considered.

events.title: Submit proofs
events.description: Rent receipts, agreements, investment statements, premium receipts, tickets and bills. The deadline is set by your employer.

events.title: TDS true-up
events.description: Claims without proof are disallowed, and any shortfall in TDS is recovered from the remaining salaries.

events.title: Receive Form 130
events.description: The new salary TDS certificate that replaces Form 16.

events.title: File your return
events.description: Claim every genuine exemption and deduction, choose your final regime, and pay any balance or claim a refund.

body.caption: Common old regime claims and the proof payroll will ask for

cells: Rent agreement, monthly rent receipts, landlord PAN if annual rent exceeds ₹1,00,000, relationship with landlord
Payments should be traceable through bank transfers
Tickets, boarding passes or invoices for domestic travel
Fare only, and only 2 journeys in the 2026 to 2029 block
Section 123 (old 80C): ELSS, PPF, life insurance, tuition fees, home loan principal
Fund statements, PPF passbook, premium receipts, school fee receipts, lender certificate
Employee PF is already known to payroll and needs no proof
Cash payments do not qualify, except for preventive health check-ups
Lender's interest certificate, lender name and PAN
Bills in your name, submitted through the flexi portal

body.title: The HRA proof trap
body.question: Kunal pays ₹9,000 a month rent in cash to his landlord, who refuses to share his PAN. Kunal submits 12 printed rent receipts. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Rejected because rent must be above ₹1,00,000 to claim HRA
Payroll asks for landlord PAN or a declaration from the landlord, and the cash payments make the claim weak
Accepted, since PAN is only needed above ₹50,000 a month
body.explanation: Annual rent of ₹1,08,000 is above ₹1,00,000, so the landlord's PAN is required, or a declaration from the landlord if he has none. Form 124 also asks for the relationship with the landlord. Cash rent with no bank trail is exactly the kind of claim that gets questioned.

children.text: Sneha's gross salary is ₹14,00,000, with basic of ₹6,00,000 and HRA of ₹3,00,000. Her ₹72,000 of employee PF is known to payroll. When no proofs arrived, payroll removed her HRA exemption, her ₹78,000 of ELSS and her ₹25,000 health insurance.

body.title: The true-up
body.prompt: Sneha's full-year tax after proofs were disallowed is ₹2,02,960. By December, ₹8,580 a month for 9 months has been deducted. If the shortfall is recovered equally from January, February and March, what is her monthly TDS in those months?
body.explanation: TDS so far = ₹8,580 × 9 = ₹77,220. Balance = ₹2,02,960 minus ₹77,220 = ₹1,25,740. Spread over 3 months = ₹41,913 a month, which is ₹33,333 more than usual.

stats.label: Extra TDS in January to March
stats.context: ₹33,333 a month on top of normal TDS

stats.label: Refund due via her return
stats.context: If she claims everything when filing

body.text: Missing the employer deadline does not cancel genuine old regime exemptions or deductions. Sneha can claim her HRA, ELSS and health insurance in her income tax return and get the ₹1,00,000 back as a refund. The real cost is cash flow: a ₹1 lakh squeeze in the last quarter, returned months later.

Flexi reimbursements are different. Phone, fuel and similar claims depend on your employer processing bills. If you miss that deadline, the amount is usually paid as taxable salary and cannot be reclaimed in your return.

children.text: Ankit worked at one company from April to September and another from October to March, earning ₹7,00,000 at each. He is in the new regime and never told his second employer about his first salary.
Employer 1 saw ₹7,00,000 minus ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹6,25,000, within the rebate. TDS: nil
Employer 2 saw the same. TDS: nil
His real taxable income: ₹14,00,000 minus one ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹13,25,000
Tax: ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + 15% of ₹1,25,000 = ₹78,750, plus cess = ₹81,900, payable when he files, with interest for late payment

body.title: Ankit's bill
body.prompt: Confirm Ankit's tax for the year on combined salary of ₹14,00,000 under the new regime, including 4% cess.
body.explanation: Taxable income = ₹14,00,000 minus ₹75,000 = ₹13,25,000. Slab tax = ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + 15% of ₹1,25,000 (₹18,750) = ₹78,750. Plus 4% cess = ₹81,900. Had he declared his previous salary in Form 122, his second employer would have deducted this through TDS.

children.text: Missing a proof vs faking one

A missed deadline costs cash flow. A fake rent receipt or an inflated claim can cost far more. Under Section 439 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 270A of the 1961 Act), the penalty is 50% of the tax on under-reported income, and 200% of the tax where income is misreported, such as through false claims or documents, on top of the tax and interest.

cards.definition: Employee's declaration of claims to the employer. Replaces Form 12BB and adds relationship with landlord.
Declaration of salary from other employers in the year, house property loss and other income. Replaces Forms 12B and 12BAA.
Salary TDS certificate issued by the employer. Replaces Form 16.
The employer's quarterly salary TDS return. Replaces Form 24Q.
TDS on salary under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Replaces Section 192.
Penalty for under-reporting (50%) and misreporting (200%) of income. Replaces Section 270A.

body.title: Name the certificate
body.textWithBlank: From tax year 2026-27, your employer's salary TDS certificate is called Form ___.
body.explanation: Form 130 replaces Form 16 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. It is generated through TRACES and has three parts, including a detailed salary computation.

body.title: Sneha's recovery plan
body.scenario: It is 20 January. Sneha has just seen the payroll notice that her claims were disallowed. Her payroll portal says the proof window has closed but "exceptional re-submissions" can be emailed to payroll until 31 January. She has all her rent receipts, bank transfers, the rent agreement, ELSS statements and the insurance receipt.
body.prompt: What should Sneha do now, and what if payroll refuses?
body.modelAnswer: First, email payroll today with every proof attached and ask for re-submission before 31 January. If accepted, her TDS will be recalculated and the January to March spike largely disappears. Second, if payroll refuses, she should plan for about ₹1,00,000 of extra TDS across three salaries: check whether any SIPs or EMIs need to be paused or covered from savings. Third, keep every document. When filing her return by 31 July 2027, she should choose the old regime and claim HRA of ₹2,40,000, Section 123 of ₹1,50,000 and Section 126 of ₹25,000. Her return will show a refund of about ₹1,00,000. Her Form 130 will show lower exemptions than her return, which is normal in this situation, but she must be able to back every claim with documents if the department asks. Finally, she should set a calendar reminder for next year's proof window in December.

body.title: Your proof kit
steps: April: declare your regime to your employer and fill Form 124 if you are in the old regime
On joining a new employer mid-year: submit Form 122 with previous salary and TDS
Every month: pay rent by bank transfer and save the receipt
Every month: upload flexi bills such as phone and fuel
Keep ELSS, PPF, insurance and tuition fee statements in one folder
December: check the proof deadline and upload everything
June: match Form 130 with your Annual Information Statement before filing
July: file your return, claiming anything payroll disallowed

body.text: Form numbers and sections are under the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026. Employer deadlines and processes vary. This lesson is for education and is not personalised tax advice.

points: The new regime is the default. Tell your employer in writing if you want TDS under the old regime.
Form 124 replaces Form 12BB for declaring claims. Form 122 reports salary from a previous employer. Form 130 replaces Form 16.
Missing the proof deadline triggers a TDS catch-up in January to March. Sneha's monthly TDS jumped from ₹8,580 to ₹41,913.
Genuine old regime exemptions and deductions can still be claimed in your return for a refund. Missed flexi reimbursements usually cannot.
After a job change, declare previous salary through Form 122 to avoid a tax bill when filing.
False claims attract penalties of up to 200% of the tax under Section 439.
